title: Char-classifier prefetch experiment log
content:
Purpose and quick summary:
This note captures a set of small experiments and microbenchmarks exploring a C-side "char classifier" that prefetches/decodes input bytes into a compact classification map (whitespace, punctuation, continuation-byte, ascii-word, high-bit) and exposes token-boundary scanning to the runtime as a single pass. The hypothesis: do more work in native code with predictable memory access to reduce Python-level loop overhead, branch misprediction, and cross-thread scheduling pressure during request preproc.

Why this is different from previous tokenizer work:
- Many earlier docs focus on tokenizer algorithm choices or moving entire tokenizers to C. This is intentionally narrow: a tiny, stable classification layer that returns token boundaries (byte offsets) instead of full subword token ids. Designed to be fast, cache-friendly, and safe to call from worker threads without holding the GIL for long.

Observed symptoms that motivated the experiment:
- Small/single-sentence requests show disproportionate CPU wall time in preproc loops (hot sampled to Python frame that does byte-by-byte class checks).
- High variance in tail p95/p99 when request rates spike; flamegraphs frequently show repeated Python frames + memcpy and occasional syscall wakes from thread-pool workers.
- Profiling indicates branch-mispredict heavy inner loops and frequent interaction with allocator arenas for temporary slices.

Experiment goals:
1) Measure baseline for boundary-detection microbench in Python (two variants: pure-Python using memoryview and CPython loop; and Python wrapping current C tokenizer code path).
2) Implement a small C extension (char_classifier) exposing: classify(buf, len) -> bitset buffer (one bit per byte: is_wordchar) and find_boundaries(prefetch_map, window_size) -> list of offsets. Prioritize single-thread reentrancy and short-run release/acquire of GIL.
3) Evaluate latency, CPU cycles per byte, branch-mispredict stats, and p50/p95/p99 for tiny requests under realistic noise.
4) Observe interaction with existing thread-pool and network-acceptor under bursty arrival.

Benchmark harness and environment:
- Machines: c6i-like dev-equivalent (8 vCPU), and a beefier 32-vCPU internal perf node.
- Python runtime: CPython 3.12 debug build (same as prod build flags), jemalloc enabled on perf node.
- Input corpus: 200k small prompts (avg 24 bytes), 50k medium prompts (avg 128 bytes), mixture injected into async worker pool.
- Load profile: Poisson arrival with mean qps=150/second and bursts to 800 qps for 500ms every 3s.
- Tools: perf record, Linux perf stat, Cachegrind for cycles/cache-miss approximation, and our in-prod microprofiler (sampling at 1ms).

Microbenchmark results (summaries):
- Baseline pure-Python scan (loop checking byte classes): ~210 cycles/byte, branch-mispredicts ~0.18 per byte, p95 latency for 24-byte request: 12.6ms under steady 150 qps.
- Python wrapper around existing C tokenizer path (current prod fast-path): ~95 cycles/byte, branch-mispredicts ~0.06 per byte, p95 6.2ms.
- New char_classifier (single-pass, 64-bit word-based scanning + table lookup) implemented in C: ~28 cycles/byte, branch-mispredicts ~0.01 per byte, p95 2.1ms.
- Overhead of converting bitset->offsets in Python if done naively removed most benefit; final design returns compact uint32 offsets in a pre-allocated buffer the caller passes in to avoid extra allocs.

Profiling notes and surprises:
- Biggest wins were from reducing Python-level loop iterations and avoiding per-request temporary object allocation. Pre-allocating buffers and returning counts + offsets removed >40% of GC pressure in the benchmark.
- SIMD-friendly scanning yielded only modest extra gains vs 64-bit narrow loops on our test CPUs; branch elimination and table-driven classification did more heavy lifting.
- Hot path still shows "context switch" lines in perf during burst spikes: likely worker wakeups due to thread pool handoff. The C classifier reduces per-request CPU time, but we still see queuing effects that need scheduler/worker tuning.
- When the classifier was implemented to always acquire the GIL for the full scan, latency regressed; releasing the GIL during the scan (and only acquiring for final buffer-write) significantly improved throughput. Need to ensure safety for buffer writes.

Interaction with thread pools and allocator:
- Two axes matter: (1) how long a worker is held busy (CPU time), (2) number of short-lived allocations. The char_classifier reduces both, but allocations dominated by returning offsets if code wasn't careful.
- On perf node with jemalloc arenas, contention for arenas appeared in CPU flamegraphs during bursts. Mitigation: use pre-allocated per-worker buffers stored in thread-local storage to avoid allocator hot-path.

Safety, correctness, and edge cases:
- Must handle UTF-8 continuation bytes robustly; classifier flags continuation bytes specially so that downstream boundary logic can treat multi-byte sequences atomically.
- For very long inputs (>128KB) we fall back to chunked scanning to keep stack/latency stable. Benchmarks didn't hit this, but production requests can be large.

Prototype API (sketch):
- cfunc int classify_bytes(const uint8_t *buf, size_t n, uint8_t *out_bitset, size_t out_capacity);
- cfunc int extract_boundaries(const uint8_t *bitset, size_t n, uint32_t *out_offsets, size_t max_offsets);
- Python wrapper: classify_and_extract(buf: bytes, offsets: bytearray) -> int(count) (releases GIL during classify/scan, acquires briefly to fill offsets buffer).

Next steps and action items:
- (Aisha) finish PR with per-worker preallocated offset buffer + tests for multi-byte UTF-8 cases (due 2025-11-14).
- (Miguel) run scaled perf job on 32-vCPU node with realistic network stacks and record 10k burst traces (due 2025-11-12).
- (Ellen) instrument thread-pool scheduling jitter and record wakeup latencies when classifier is enabled vs baseline (due 2025-11-13).
- (Ravi) propose thread-pool tuning: bump acceptor thread priority, experiment with handing off socket accepts via lockless queue to tokenizer workers (due 2025-11-18).

Questions for discussion:
- Do we accept a native dependency for the hosted API runner? Tradeoffs between reduced CPU cost vs packaging complexity for customers (Dedicated/Private must bundle).
- Is returning offsets enough for downstream processing (tokenizer) to avoid re-scan? We should prototype a combined pass that returns subword tokens for the most common model BPE to measure end-to-end benefit.

Quick conclusion:
A small, well-scoped native char-classifier that focuses on prefetch-friendly byte scanning and returning offsets yields large reductions in per-byte cycles and p95 latency for small requests in our bench harness. The bulk of remaining tail artifacts come from scheduling/allocator interactions rather than raw parse cost. Follow-ups: finalize safe GIL-release implementation, integrate with per-worker storage (avoid allocs), and run scaled burst experiments to validate system-level tail behavior.

Appendix: quick command snippets used
- perf stat -e cycles,branch-misses,cache-references,cache-misses -r 5 python -m perf_harness --qps 150 --burst 800 --samples 5
- perf record -F 99 -a -- python -m perf_harness --scenario small_prompts --duration 120
- Cachegrind (approx): valgrind --tool=cachegrind -- cachegrind python -m perf_harness --scenario small_prompts

End of note.
